title: Traversing a Collection by Its Values

blocks.text: for (int valor : datos) visits the elements of datos in their existing order. On each iteration, it creates a variable valor initialized with a copy of the current element. The colon separates the name of that variable from the collection. It is neither a comparison condition nor a separator from a counter-based for loop.
The output is 4;2;7;. The body runs three times. There is no need to calculate indices to visit every element; a range-based loop expresses that intention directly.

blocks.text: Changing a copy does not change the vector

In for (int valor : datos), valor is a different object from the element. The statement valor += 1; changes that copy during the iteration. It can affect what is printed inside the body, but the values in datos remain unchanged. At the end of the iteration, that local variable is no longer available; the next iteration obtains another copy.

blocks.question: You want all elements to remain incremented in the vector. Is changing valor in for (int valor : datos) enough?

No: that changes a copy; you must access the elements to modify them.
Only if there are two elements.
blocks.explanation: Recall the difference between copying a value and retaining access to the original object.
